look_here_first: 1) Older trunks have unusually smooth pale gray peeling/mottled bark; 2) leaves are SMALL (often 1.5–3.5 cm), simple, alternate, usually obovate with rolled-under margins and short hairs beneath; 3) immature berries green, RIPE fruits dark purple-black with persistent calyx. Never identify from black fruit alone.
project_tracker_diagnostic: Small shrub/tree with smooth mottled peeling bark, small alternate obovate leaves with tomentose undersides, urn-shaped white flowers, and dark to black pubescent berries with a persistent calyx.

morphology_keys.habit: Shrub to small tree, often multistemmed; foliage may be deciduous or persistent depending on site.
morphology_keys.bark: Smooth pale gray to reddish-gray bark that exfoliates and creates a mottled trunk.
morphology_keys.leaves: Alternate simple leaves, usually small and obovate, glossy/dark above and densely tomentose beneath.
morphology_keys.reproductive: White urn-shaped flowers; flowers arise on previous-season twigs and ovaries are pubescent.
morphology_keys.fruit: Berrylike fruit roughly 1.5–2.5 cm, maturing dark/black and remaining pubescent, with persistent calyx and several seeds.
morphology_keys.joey_field_note: Joey's desert-field frame gives an immediate woody-ID view of Texas persimmon's smooth pale bark and small-tree habit. Use the bark as an early cue, then confirm the small obovate leaves and, when present, the pubescent black fruit.
morphology_keys.leaf_field_details: UT Austin Williamson flora: simple alternate blades approximately 15–35 × 7–16 mm (local specimens), obovate/elliptic, rounded or notched apex, frequently rolled-under (revolute) margin, short-tomentose underside.
morphology_keys.flower_field_details: Small white to cream 5-lobed urn flowers; pollen-producing flowers typically in 1–3-flower clusters, ovary-bearing flowers often solitary. A source conflict exists over dioecious vs monoecious organization; identify flower sex from visible organs rather than assume tree sex.
morphology_keys.berry_field_details: Young fruit green; mature 17–22 mm berry black/dark purple, often hairy, with persistent conspicuous 4–5-lobed calyx and typically several hard brown seeds.

comparisons.key_distinctions: American persimmon usually has much larger leaves, flowers on current-season growth, and glabrous yellow-orange to dark-red fruit. Texas persimmon has much smaller tomentose leaves and pubescent black fruit.

ecological_notes.habitat: Rocky limestone slopes, arroyos, ravines, uplands and mature woody/riparian communities across central and southern Texas.
ecological_notes.learning_note: An excellent woody-ID species because bark, leaves and fruit all supply independent confirmation characters.

visual_comparison.title: Recognize Texas persimmon from bark, leaf edges and berries
visual_comparison.subtitle: Start with smooth pale trunks, then tiny leathery leaves. Fruit color helps when berries are ripe—but not every tree is fruiting.
visual_comparison.memory_rule: SMOOTH PALE BARK + SMALL DOWN-CURLED LEAVES + BLACK RIPE BERRIES.

items.image_role: smooth pale to dark-gray mottled trunks
items.caption: These mature stems are smooth, unlike the thick square-blocked bark of American persimmon. Smooth bark is age-dependent; saplings may be less obvious.

reproductive_system_source_conflict.status: SOURCE-CONFLICT; treat as unsettled pending specimen/voucher study
reproductive_system_source_conflict.most_sources: USDA FEIS and NPSOT call D. texana dioecious (male vs female individual trees).
reproductive_system_source_conflict.contrary_treatment: A. C. Gibson, UT Austin Vascular Plants of Williamson County explicitly calls D. texana monoecious while distinguishing staminate and pistillate flowers.
reproductive_system_source_conflict.learner_instruction: Teach staminate versus pistillate structure, and fruiting only on plants bearing functional female flowers. Do NOT claim every individual is strictly male or strictly female without checking the population.
